doc.title: Dave Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Race, trad jazz and New Orleans brass bands after Katrina
summary: Dave discusses why trad is mostly played by white bands, the Dirty Dozen's influence, and Rowe's pre-Katrina brass band memory.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Is there some kind of racial thing with black musicians nowadays being — not playing traditional jazz? It seems like most of the bands I see are all white that do it.

Well yeah, I would say so. I think outside of New Orleans this kind of music is really foreign to the culture but that goes for white and black students and Hispanics and Asian and what have you. This has just pretty much fallen off the radar screen. But yeah I mean as everybody knows a great disproportionate share of the innovations in this music have come from African-American artists. And I think the music of the African-American community is now very far removed from this kind of thing, except in New Orleans, where this kind of music is heard on the streets, even post-Katrina. It’s struggling but it’s still there. It’s going to come back. But it’s a kind of a normal part of life down there. But having said that, even down there young musicians, and I’m told from those who live there, particularly young African-American musicians, are more interested in moving forward from that taking for instance the whole neo-brass band movement, the Dirty Dozen and all the bands that they’ve inspired. In fact I would say probably most brass bands down there today are built more on the Dirty Dozen model than on the original sound. And what I mean by that is the Dirty Dozen took the brass band instrumentation and really completely changed the sound of it — used contemporary phrasing. The Dirty Dozen of course plays, you can hear them playing hip hop and funk and all kinds of stuff that has very little relation to traditional brass band sound at all except that it has a sousaphone in there somewhere. And that’s all good too. But I think most young players, and I’m told most African-American players in that city are kind of more drawn towards that — and there’s very little even there, very little participation by young people in this music. So New Orleans is particularly — New Orleans teachers — the Park in there has told me that New Orleans teachers have expressed a big interest in this. So I hope having these kinds of materials will help bring it back not only in the city where it all started but across the country.
My wife and I were in New Orleans just before Katrina actually on a vacation. We heard the most amazing group of — I guess teenagers on the corner playing in a brass band. I was just —
Was it sort of a funky style brass band or a traditional brass band?

I think it was more traditional, although the next time we heard them, the next night, they were playing an arrangements of “Stand By Me,” the Ben E. King song. But they were wailing. You could hear them for blocks.
